1.0.0.en: The content of Paul's letter is evident from the apostolic greeting at the beginning of his epistles. As he addresses the Thessalonians, who were suffering persecution from the unbelieving Jews, he shows his love and humility, and does not call himself an Apostle, since this was already known to them.

1.0.1.en: He joins with himself his two disciples, Silvanus (Silas) and Timothy, in sending the greeting to them, although he alone is the writer of the letter, for those who are afflicted need the sympathy of many.

1.0.2.en: He shows the fatherhood of God when he says "God our Father," so that they might feel His care for them, and likewise Christ the Savior, who unites the believers, Gentiles and Jews, in one Church. And he sends them the grace of God, which is able to give them an inner peace that the outward afflictions they suffer cannot take away.

1.0.3.en: If St. Paul writes to the Thessalonians, who suffered persecution from unbelievers, in order to encourage them with grace and peace, then may you take care to encourage everyone who is in distress or suffering, whether a small child or a grown person, because your fatherly care and encouragement inspire him to bear sufferings with patience and courage, and you yourself are filled with it, so that you too are strengthened by the grace of God.

1.1.s.en: (2) Thanksgiving to God for their faith, love and hope

1.1.0.en: The Apostle encourages them to endure sufferings by praising their virtues, saying: we give thanks to God for the fruits of grace that abound in you, for God is the source of all goodness in men.

1.1.1.en: It was the Apostle's custom to spend long hours in prayer for the Churches, and for the particular need of each Church.

1.1.2.en: Perhaps we turn to the Lord to pray for our brethren in circumstances of grief, danger and sickness, but it is beautiful to return to Him with thanksgiving for His grace in those who are being saved, and also to pray if they suffer from the weakness of their spiritual condition.

1.2.0.en: Here the Apostle mentions the three virtues that are the fruit of the work of grace in them, but he does not speak here of the virtues themselves, but of their results, namely the work of faith, the labor of love, the patience of hope. Work of your faith: that is, fruitful, active and effective faith, by which the reality of our faith is shown before God, "for faith without works is dead" (Jas 2:26). Labor of your love: true love is a sacrificial love, which labors for the sake of others and in the service of the brethren.

1.2.1.en: Patience of your hope: hope grants consolation in sorrow and gives patience in affliction, and the Lord Jesus, to Him be the glory, is Himself the hope who gives the strength to endure, and He is also the example in patience.

1.3.0.en: St. Paul knew that the fruit of the Spirit which appeared in their lives was the proof of the new life that is in Christ, and so they had become chosen according to the foreknowledge of God, and had become a people set apart and consecrated by God to be the object of His love. On this basis St. Paul sets aside the Jews' idea that they are the chosen people, to put in its place the spiritual election of those who believe in Christ (Gal 6:16), and also to give them encouragement, as he affirms God's election of them.

1.4.s.en: (3) Their faith an example to others

1.4.0.en: What manner of men: how greatly Paul and his disciples bore the labors of the ministry, in spiritual manliness and with much self-sacrifice.

1.4.1.en: For your sake: to win your souls.

1.4.2.en: Paul makes clear that his preaching of the Gospel in Thessalonica was not in word only, but he delivered it to them in confidence and faith and in the power of the Holy Spirit working in him, and he endured afflictions and labor in preaching in order to draw their souls to Christ.

1.5.0.en: The life of Paul and his companions, with self-denial and holy conduct, left a deep impression on the souls of the Thessalonians, so they imitated them. They received the word in much affliction and suffered bitter persecution, yet they were joyful in the message that told them of the forgiveness of their sins and the hope of eternal life. The saying applied to them: "as sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing" (2 Cor 6:10).

1.6.0.en: Macedonia: the northern part of Greece.

1.6.1.en: Achaia: the southern part of Greece.

1.6.2.en: The change in their lives was so great that others quickly noticed it, and they became "ensamples" to all who were in Macedonia and who received the faith as they did in the north, and also in Achaia in the south. Their lives bore witness that they were in a living relationship with God, and they were true lights in the darkness of the world.

1.7.0.en: The believers in Thessalonica were a living witness to the power of life with Christ, so their report sounded forth like a trumpet not only in Macedonia and Achaia but also in every direction, and this not because of miracles they performed but because of their faith in God. Thessalonica was an important commercial center, so the news spread from that center to every place. And before the greatness of their faith, Paul found no words with which to glorify their faith, because it had become plain to all.

1.8.0.en: When St. Paul preached in the various lands of Greece, he found them marveling at the Thessalonians' acceptance of his message and their turning from the worship of idols to the worship of God; indeed, they hastened to tell St. Paul of this, which helped the other lands to receive the faith and to stand firm in Christ.

1.9.0.en: The Thessalonians await the Second Coming of the Lord, which is the hope of all Christianity and by which the divine promises are fulfilled in eternal life. For the One whom they await is the very One who died for them, and we await Him as Savior, after He reconciled us with God the Father by the Cross, to change the form of the body of our humility so that it may be in the likeness of the body of His glory (Phil 3:21). This too is a new encouragement that every suffering is followed by great glory, as happened to our Lord Jesus Christ, who bore the sufferings of salvation and then sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high.

1.9.1.en: Know, my brother, that your enduring of the faith with thanksgiving, and your holding fast to your principles in spite of afflictions, not only brings an abundance of God's blessings upon you but also influences those around you more than any words.

2.0.0.en: For you yourselves, brethren, know that our coming among you was not in vain, not only because our coming among you, we the servants of Christ, had a great effect at that time, but also because our work was afterward shown to be firm, deeply rooted and successful, for the fruits continued and increased.

2.1.0.en: The bodily sufferings that befell us in Philippi, such as beating, imprisonment and the tearing of garments, and the moral sufferings of contempt and scorn, did not keep us from coming to you and boldly proclaiming the Gospel, whatever persecution we met, for the faithful servants of Christ do not draw back, because they count themselves unworthy to be dishonored for His name's sake.

2.2.0.en: For our preaching is not falsehood but assured truth, nor is it from an impure mind aiming at selfish ends, nor in craftiness to hide something for a purpose of one's own, but with all frankness and plainness.

2.3.0.en: For God chose us by His grace and entrusted us with preaching in His name, with all that this includes of the highest degrees of responsibility, so we serve to please God and not to please men at the expense of the pleasure of God, who searches the hearts and tests the thoughts.

2.4.0.en: You yourselves bear witness that we did not use words such as the flattery of men requires when they have some purpose of their own, and we did not speak smooth words or gentle phrases out of greed and love of money and desire for shameful gain. And while the Thessalonians can bear witness to all this concerning his outward conduct, there is another witness to the inner thought, known to God, who knows the secrets of hearts.

2.5.0.en: Dignity as apostles of Christ: St. Paul toiled and worked with his own hands to meet his personal needs, although he was not bound to do so and it was his right that they should provide for his needs, like the rest of Christ's disciples who preach in the various lands.

2.5.1.en: True servants of God do not seek their own glory, but hide themselves so as to show Christ, as John the Baptist said, "He must increase, but I must decrease" (Jn 3:30). The Apostle did not use his apostolic authority except where it was necessary, and he sought nothing to please himself, but his only aim was the glory of God.

2.6.0.en: Paul shows that he and his disciples were gentle and tender, and with all meekness, humility and love they sat in the midst of their brethren in full familiarity, as a nursing mother sits with her little ones around her, holding them to her breast in tenderness.

2.7.0.en: Thus they treated them with all tenderness and love, giving every effort for their edification in Christ, giving them not only the Gospel of God but their own selves also, for they were ready to lay down their lives for them as Christ did for us all, all this out of their love for them.

2.8.0.en: The Apostle reminds them of the striving and sufferings they bore for the sake of their edification, and during their preaching they worked with their hands to meet their needs without burdening them. The Apostle offered the Gospel freely so that there might be no blemish on the ministry, although it was his right to live of the Gospel because he proclaimed the Gospel. Paul worked at the trade of tent-making.

2.8.1.en: The Apostle also makes clear that ministry is not merely teaching, but also upbringing, with every follow-up and effort, so that the one served may reach spiritual success.

2.8.2.en: If you are a servant, a father or a mother, may you be tender toward those you serve and ready to lay down your life for them as Christ did with you. Look at His body given for you on the altar every day, so that you may be eager to sacrifice for those you serve, knowing that they need your love as nursing infants need the one who brings them up, and trust that God's reward to you is great and the tenderness He will pour out upon you exceeds all your expectations.

2.9.s.en: (2) His fatherhood and purity in ministry

2.9.0.en: Men can judge only the outward conduct, so besides asking for their witness to his conduct, he also calls God to witness for him. For the righteous man is not merely one who does works of righteousness, but one who does works of righteousness in a mind befitting a righteous man. Here the Apostle enumerates the aspects of his conduct, which are:

2.9.3.en: Unblameably: that is, without anyone reproving him for a fault he commits.

2.10.0.en: As you saw how we offered our spiritual exhortation to each one of you with all sincerity, as a father counsels his children, and we encouraged you to walk worthy of God and worthy of the calling to which you were called.

2.11.0.en: Charged: here this means the aspect of warning and admonition.

2.11.1.en: When the Thessalonians worshiped idols, they walked as befits idols, but when they returned to the true God, their walk became as befits God, who accomplished salvation for them through His Son and opened to them the gates of eternal glory in His Kingdom.

2.11.2.en: Thus the warmth of the Apostle's heart is made plain, as he follows each one individually with real concern like a father with his children, and after showing them his fatherhood, he calls them to upright Christian conduct, and so the servant should be.

2.11.3.en: Do not seek your own interest or comfort when you serve God, whether in your care for your children or in your service in the Church. Be pure in your words and thoughts so that you may be pleasing before God and not cause those you serve or bring up to stumble. Care for every individual and show him your love, so that he is not lost in the crowd but is strengthened, however weak he may be.

2.12.0.en: After St. Paul spoke about himself and his disciples in verses (1-12), he turns to speak about the Thessalonians in verses (13, 14). The Apostle begins by giving thanks to God for the Thessalonians' entering into the faith. In this he teaches us always to give the credit to God, who crowns our works with success, and not to ourselves, and that thanksgiving should always be in our lives. The Thessalonians received the word not as the word of men, that is, of Paul, Silas and Timothy, but as the word of God, with all reverence, awe and faith.

2.12.1.en: Through Paul and his disciples they heard the voice of God Himself and His message calling them to eternal life, and the word of God working in them, cleansing and purifying them.

2.12.2.en: Studying the word of God reveals to us our spiritual condition, so if we are diligent and persistent in studying it, our lives will be pure and pleasing to the Lord. May we take care each day to read a portion of the Holy Bible and choose a verse to apply in our lives, so that it will reveal some of our faults and direct us in the path of spiritual growth.

2.13.0.en: In Christ Jesus: an expression St. Paul uses in many of his epistles, by which he means union and fellowship with Christ, like the union of the head with the members of the body, which is His Church. You have suffered from the Gentiles around you who rejected the faith, just as the Church of Jerusalem also suffered from the Jews who did not believe. The Christian, whether of Jewish or Gentile origin, is persecuted, because Satan is against him and stirs up the wicked against him. Here we see also the unity of sufferings, just as there is also the unity of fruits and reward. Thus it is clear that there is no preaching or faith without suffering, so that no one should be troubled.

2.14.0.en: The Jews seized Christ and handed Him over to the Gentile Romans, who killed Him, so they were considered the killers; and likewise they killed their prophets, as the Lord Christ said of them, "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee..." (Mt 23:37). And now they persecute us, the Apostles, and do not care to please God, although they pretend that this is their task and calling. They are enemies of all mankind, for God distinguished them from the Gentiles who worship idols by making them a special people for Himself, to be an example to the rest of the peoples and to draw them to the faith; but on the contrary they killed the prophets and Christ Himself and became a bad example, so they hid the light of God from the world and in this became opposed to it, and in their pride they despised the other peoples and races.

2.15.0.en: The Jews do not want the salvation of the Gentiles, but despise them and regard them as dogs, and do not want the message of salvation and their share in the Messiah to reach them, and want eternal destruction to come upon all the Gentiles. This is the secret of their hatred toward Paul, because he proclaimed Jesus Christ to the pagans, saying that God is the God of the Jews and the Gentiles. They killed the prophets, then the Lord Jesus, and persecuted the Apostles, and so on until they fill up the measure of their evil, as was their way in ancient times. But God turned their persecution of the Apostles and their refusal of the message into the directing of the Gospel to the Gentiles who accepted the faith, so evil was turned into good by the providential work of God. But the Jews, because of the blood of the prophets which stains their life and history, and especially because of the blood of Christ, brought upon themselves the guilt of blood, and so the wrath of God came upon them. This appeared in the Romans' persecution of them until they destroyed Jerusalem in the year 70 AD, and persecutions continued to overtake them.

2.15.1.en: Enduring sufferings is difficult, but it is a proof of our sonship to God, because it is a fellowship in His sufferings and a declaration of our love for Him. May we accept with thanksgiving the afflictions that come upon us, on condition that we are not at fault in anything.

2.16.0.en: In this verse we meet the overflowing love expressed in the abundant emotions of St. Paul, as he speaks of his intense longing for them and his urgent desire to see them, after being absent from them from the time he was with them until he wrote this letter to them, a period of about four months; but his absence from them was in body while their hearts remained bound together, for he remembered them without ceasing in his prayers.

2.17.0.en: He strove with all sincere desire to find a way to come to them and see them, and he tried this more than once, but Satan hindered him from coming to them through the opposing Jews. Here a question arises: can Satan hinder the work of the Lord and His servants? The answer is yes. He stirs up persecution against them and obstructs them.

2.17.1.en: The second question: does Satan act as he pleases? The answer: no, for he works within the limits that the Lord permits him, so Satan's success in anything also depends on the will of God.

2.18.0.en: The Apostle shows the place of the Thessalonians in his heart, and declares to them that his service to them is what gives him the crown and the glory in the day of judgment and joy before Christ our Lord.

2.18.1.en: Take care to express your feelings of love for others so as to overcome the thoughts of doubt or faint-heartedness that may fight against them. All people need encouragement, especially since Satan continually creates misunderstanding in various forms, so we must overcome him by showing continual love to all who are around us.
